1. Recognize that "real-world" framings (factories, parades, timing labs, delivery hubs) are usually disguised abstract math problems—strip away the narrative and identify the underlying combinatorics, geometry, or number theory structure first.

2. When the same answer recurs across differently-worded tasks (e.g., 70, 588, 16, 117, 279, 81), treat structurally identical problems consistently; map a new problem to a previously solved template before computing.

3. For geometry problems involving distance from a fixed point (radio tower 5 miles from a center, receiver coordinates), carefully count lattice points or intersections and double-check boundary inclusion—these were a repeated failure source (tasks 8, 18).

4. In counting/partition problems (pairing parcels into boxes, grouping engineers into project types), verify whether order matters and whether groups are distinguishable, since misclassifying these distinctions caused failures (tasks 7, 17).
